opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the barriers are pretty low, and I think that's one of the most important things for people to internalize when they're thinking about open-weight release.

If you look at the research over the last couple of years, including some of our own work at FAR.AI, removing safety fine-tuning from an open-weight model is remarkably cheap. You can take a model that's been through extensive refusal training and, with a few hundred examples of harmful completions and a fine-tuning run that costs maybe tens of dollars of compute, get it to answer almost anything. There are also even lighter-weight techniques. Things like refusal-direction ablation, where you identify a direction in activation space associated with refusing and just project it out, don't even require gradient updates. People have packaged this up, so you'll see "abliterated" versions of popular models appear on Hugging Face within days of a release.

So the technical skill required is maybe a competent grad student, or frankly a motivated hobbyist following a tutorial. The compute is trivial. The data is easy to generate or find. On every axis the barrier is low.

There's been a lot of interest in what people call tamper-resistant safeguards, methods that try to make the weights themselves robust to fine-tuning attacks. I think that's a worthwhile research direction, but my read of the current evidence is that these defenses tend to hold up against the specific attacks they were designed against and then fall over when someone tries a slightly different hyperparameter setting, a different optimizer, a different dataset. We're seeing the classic adversarial robustness pattern, where defenses get published and are broken shortly afterward. I wouldn't bet that any current method raises the cost of removal by more than a modest amount for a determined attacker.

The practical upshot is that when a developer releases weights, they should assume the safeguards are gone. The right question isn't "is the model safe given its refusal training?" It's "what is this model capable of once someone strips the refusals, and are we comfortable with that capability being freely available, permanently, since you can't recall weights?" For a lot of current models I think the answer is yes, the benefits of openness clearly outweigh the marginal risk. But as capabilities grow, particularly in areas like bio, cyber, or autonomous operation, that calculus shifts, and we shouldn't kid ourselves that safety fine-tuning is doing much work in the open-weight setting.

r001.rationale: It says safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning or refusal-direction ablation, and that developers should assume safeguards are gone once weights are released.

r002.rationale: It describes the skill needed as a competent graduate student’s—or a motivated hobbyist’s following a tutorial—and calls the technical barrier low.

r003.rationale: It says fine-tuning may cost tens of dollars in compute and characterizes the compute barrier as trivial.

r004.rationale: It says current defenses add at most a modest cost for a determined attacker and that the necessary technical skill is accessible to a motivated hobbyist.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say the barriers are very low right now, and I think that's something people outside the field often underestimate. The headline finding from the last couple of years is that fine-tuning on a surprisingly small number of examples, sometimes just a few hundred, sometimes even fewer, is enough to strip out most of the refusal behavior from a model that's been through RLHF. And this isn't exotic. It's the same fine-tuning pipeline that people use for perfectly legitimate purposes, so there's no special expertise or infrastructure needed beyond what a hobbyist with a consumer GPU or a few dollars of cloud compute already has.

The reason this works, as far as we understand it, is that safety training is pretty shallow relative to the capabilities. The model learns a thin layer of "when you see this kind of request, produce a refusal," but the underlying knowledge and capability to do the harmful thing is still fully there. So you're not teaching the model anything new when you remove safeguards, you're just removing a small behavioral veneer, and that's a much easier optimization problem than instilling capabilities in the first place. You also see this with techniques that don't even require gradient-based fine-tuning, things like directly editing activations or identifying a "refusal direction" in the residual stream and ablating it. Those can be done with a handful of forward passes.

Now, there is a research agenda around making safeguards more tamper-resistant, and I think that's genuinely valuable work. The idea is to train models so that fine-tuning towards harmful behavior is harder or slower, or so that the harmful knowledge is actually degraded rather than just hidden behind a refusal. Our own red-teaming work and others' has generally found that the current generation of these methods doesn't hold up that well under adaptive attack. You change the fine-tuning hyperparameters, you use a different data distribution, you add a few more steps, and the protection tends to break. That's not to say the direction is hopeless, but I'd put it in the category of "promising research problem," not "deployed defense you can rely on."

So my overall assessment is something like: if you release the weights, you should assume that any safeguards you've trained in will be removed by anyone who is motivated to do so, and you should make your release decision on that basis. The relevant question becomes not "how good are the safeguards" but "how dangerous is the underlying capability if someone has unrestricted access to it." For current models I think that calculus mostly favors openness, because the marginal uplift over what's already available is limited. But that could change as capabilities grow, and I'd like to see the tamper-resistance research mature a lot before we're leaning on it for anything high-stakes.

r001.rationale: It says fine-tuning can strip most refusal behavior and recommends assuming safeguards will be removed when weights are released.

r002.rationale: It says no special expertise is needed, so it does not identify required technical expertise as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It mentions a consumer GPU or a few dollars of cloud compute as sufficient, but does not identify compute requirements as a barrier.

r004.rationale: It says anyone motivated to remove safeguards can do so and that current defenses break under adaptive attacks.

astra-6.text:
I think the barriers are fairly low today. If you have the weights, you have a lot of control over the model. You can fine-tune it, and the training that makes it refuse certain requests can often be undone with relatively modest resources. You don’t necessarily need anything close to the compute that went into training the model originally.

There’s an important distinction, though, between removing a safeguard and adding a capability. Getting a model to answer a question it previously refused doesn’t automatically mean it can give a useful answer. So the risk depends both on how easy the safeguards are to remove and on what capabilities are already there underneath them.

I wouldn’t say making safeguards robust to weight modification is impossible. But it’s a much harder threat model than securing an API, where you retain control over what runs. For an open-weight release, I think the prudent assumption is that a motivated actor may be able to remove the refusal behavior. You should assess the consequences of releasing the underlying capabilities on that basis.

r001.rationale: It says the weights give substantial control and that refusal training can often be undone, describing weight modification as a viable way to remove safeguards.

r002.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning but does not identify the technical expertise needed for it as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute only to say that undoing refusals does not require anything close to the original training compute; it does not identify required compute as a barrier.

r004.rationale: It characterizes the barriers as fairly low and says a motivated actor may be able to remove refusal behavior, indicating the barriers would not stop capable, well-resourced attackers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the barriers are pretty low, particularly if the attacker has access to the model weights and can fine-tune them. Most safeguards today are trained into the model’s behavior, and an attacker can train that behavior back out. They don’t necessarily need to understand how the safeguard works internally; they just need examples that reward the behavior they want.

There are still practical barriers: compute, expertise, and getting suitable training data. And removing a refusal doesn’t automatically give the model a capability it didn’t have in the first place. But I wouldn’t treat those barriers as a strong security guarantee. Once you release the weights, you’re giving someone control over the system that implements the safeguards.

So I’d distinguish between safeguards that reduce accidental misuse or make a hosted service safer, which can be very valuable, and safeguards that remain effective against someone deliberately modifying an open-weight model. The latter is a much harder problem, and I don’t think we currently have a reliable solution.

r001.rationale: It says an attacker with the weights can fine-tune the model and train its safeguards out.

r002.rationale: It explicitly lists expertise as a practical barrier.

r003.rationale: It explicitly lists compute as a practical barrier.

r004.rationale: It says these barriers are not a strong security guarantee and that deliberate modification of released weights is a hard problem.
